name: Pantoprazole + Domperidone
meta: Pantoprazole Sodium: Proton pump inhibitor (PPI); Domperidone: Peripheral dopamine D2 antagonist (prokinetic / antiemetic)
Schedule H – prescription only; Domperidone: Schedule H – prescription only
sections: White to off-white crystalline powder (sodium sesquihydrate), freely soluble in water.
White or almost white powder, practically insoluble in water.

Pantoprazole Sodium: Has lower affinity for CYP enzymes than omeprazole, giving fewer drug interactions; preferred PPI with clopidogrel. First approval/introduction: Research began 1985 (Byk Gulden); Germany 1994; US FDA 2000 (Wyeth). Domperidone: In 2014 the EMA restricted use to relief of nausea and vomiting at a maximum of 10 mg three times daily, generally for ≤1 week, because of cardiac risks. First approval/introduction: Synthesised 1974 (Janssen Pharmaceutica); marketed 1979 (Switzerland, West Germany); not approved in the USA.
Pantoprazole suppresses acid secretion; domperidone (sustained release) improves gastric emptying and LES tone, relieving regurgitation, bloating and nausea.

Pantoprazole Sodium Irreversibly inhibits H+/K+-ATPase in gastric parietal cells, suppressing basal and stimulated acid secretion. Receptor / target profile: Prodrug activated in acidic canaliculi; covalently binds cysteine residues of H+/K+-ATPase.

Domperidone Blocks peripheral D2 receptors in the upper GI tract (increasing oesophageal sphincter tone and gastric emptying) and in the chemoreceptor trigger zone (outside the blood–brain barrier). Receptor / target profile: Peripherally selective D2 and D3 antagonist; acts on the chemoreceptor trigger zone (outside the blood–brain barrier) and upper GI tract; raises prolactin.
Summary: Bioavailability ~77%; Tmax 2–3 h (enteric-coated). ~98% protein bound. Metabolised by CYP2C19 and CYP3A4. Half-life ~1 h (effect lasts >24 h).
Summary: Bioavailability ~15% (first-pass); Tmax ~1 h (SR prolonged). ~92% protein bound. Metabolised by CYP3A4. Half-life 7–9 h.
GERD not responding to PPI alone
Functional dyspepsia with acid-related symptoms, bloating and early satiety
One capsule once daily before breakfast
Limit duration (domperidone cardiac safety); review within 1–2 weeks
Dose to be individualised by the treating physician according to clinical response and tolerability.
Severe: max 20 mg/day (some labels 40 mg alternate days).
EE with GERD ≥5 years: 20–40 mg/day by weight.
Severe: reduce frequency to once or twice daily.
>60 years: higher arrhythmia risk – use lowest dose.
≥12 years and ≥35 kg: adult dosing; younger: 0.25 mg/kg up to three times daily (specialist).
Excreted in small amounts; use with caution.
Hypersensitivity to pantoprazole or substituted benzimidazoles
Known QT prolongation, significant electrolyte disturbance, underlying cardiac disease (e.g. heart failure)
Concomitant QT-prolonging drugs or strong CYP3A4 inhibitors
Long-term use: hypomagnesaemia, vitamin B12 deficiency, fractures
C. difficile diarrhoea, subacute cutaneous lupus
Serious ventricular arrhythmia and sudden cardiac death – risk higher >60 years and >30 mg/day; use lowest dose, max ~1 week
Raised prolactin – galactorrhoea, gynaecomastia, menstrual irregularity
Drugs needing gastric acid for absorption (ketoconazole, atazanavir, iron salts)
Strong CYP3A4 inhibitors (ketoconazole, clarithromycin, ritonavir) – contraindicated
Pantoprazole Sodium: Magnesium on long-term use; B12 on long-term use.
Domperidone: ECG if cardiac risk factors; potassium, magnesium.
Pantoprazole Sodium: Supportive care. Domperidone: Drowsiness, disorientation, EPS (especially children), arrhythmias. ECG monitoring; supportive care.
Evidence derives from component trials; combination used for GERD with dysmotility.
Swallow whole – do not crush or chew
Do not use long-term without review
Use for the shortest time (usually ≤1 week)
Inform doctor of all heart medicines and antifungals/antibiotics
Store below 30°C in a dry place, protected from light and moisture. Keep out of the reach of children. Do not use after the expiry date.
